entry.title: Social Summary: November 28, 2026
entry.summary:
Community energy centered on a knowledge-preservation fight and a debate over AI's societal payoff. Andriy Burkov mirroring a withdrawn ML book triggered the day's biggest controversy, while Ethan Mollick argued cheap AI makes personalized help at scale a solvable problem.

  • Clement Delangue (Hugging Face) posted twice on open-source health: post-training open models to frontier quality, and distillation as a check on power concentration
  • François Chollet dismissed viral claims of record 2026 math progress as engagement farming, even as ChatGPT-generated Lean proof demos circulated
  • swyx framed a Google resurgence around new leadership talent and Gemini-4-Neon as the hottest frontier model
  • Evaluation culture drew scrutiny: a viral RPG-style 'stat sheet' proposal challenged leaderboards, and levelsio exposed the economics of AI reply-bot spam on X
  • Notable moments: Yann LeCun's viral Lisp quip, Karpathy on digital twins, plus a NVIDIA NeurIPS spotlight (Test-time Baking) and Cohere Labs' CulturalRiddles benchmark

Sentiment: genuine optimism about AI's practical upside, paired with rising skepticism toward hype, leaderboard culture, and platform manipulation.

entry.title: Social Summary: November 27, 2026

entry.title: Social Summary: November 26, 2026
entry.summary:
AGI timelines and AI governance dominated the day. Shane Legg (DeepMind co-founder) now puts the odds above 50% of Minimal AGI arriving before 2028, while Dario Amodei forcefully rejected claims that he endorses surrendering human free will to AI, igniting a wider debate over democratic oversight of frontier labs.

  • Frontier-lab scrutiny intensified: Axios reporting suggests Anthropic and OpenAI hold internal models their own staff fear, and Greg Brockman amplified a claimed proof that the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4 — a potential compute-cost landmark
  • Product momentum continued: Sam Altman announced Private Inference testing under OpenAI Private Intelligence, Perplexity unveiled Time Machine for showing models historical web states, and Hugging Face shipped Nightwatch to counter agent-driven Hub attacks
  • Evaluation culture matured: Artificial Analysis launched the FrontierPhysics leaderboard and found VLA models systematically favor the right arm, while Eugene Yan flagged persistent benchmark bugs and Jason Wei argued test-time compute remains the field's north star

Sentiment blended excitement over capability signals (AGI odds, math breakthroughs, Rust-scale engineering) with unease about safety oversight and concentration of frontier power. Ethan Mollick speculating on regulated-closed futures and Yann LeCun pushing back on genome-complexity arguments added depth.

entry.title: No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to su...
entry.summary: Dario Amodei (Anthropic CEO) publicly rebutts the suggestion that he advocates surrendering human free will to AI systems. He argues his extensive writing consistently calls for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes, draws a parallel to historical arguments for autocracy over democracy, and states that arguments against autocracy apply equally to turning governance over to AI. Massive engagement: ~6.6M views, 17k+ likes, and unusually high reply count (4.4k), indicating an active public controversy.

entry.title:
New Anthropic Fellows research: Returning to the neuron basis for interpretability
Understanding wh...
entry.summary: Anthropic announces Fellows research revisiting neuron-level interpretability. The team re-examined three classic reasons the field abandoned neuron-based analysis (polysemantic neurons, concept drift across layers, distributed facts) by measuring each neuron's contribution to outputs rather than its activation triggers. All three problems proved smaller than assumed: neurons rarely combine unrelated concepts, outputs are semantically consistent across layers, and distributed facts remain readable.

entry.title: Launching Harness Comparisons on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index: the best harness varies...
entry.summary: Artificial Analysis announces a new Harness Comparisons feature on its Coding Agent Index, showing that agent harness choice significantly affects model performance and cost. Running GPT-6 Luna and GLM-5.3-Flash across 13 harnesses reveals no single best harness: GPT-6 Luna peaks in Codex while GLM-5.3-Flash peaks in Claude Code, and best performance-per-dollar harnesses differ per model.

entry.title:
All intelligent systems I've ever seen have exactly two adaptation timescales.
The first one is on-...
entry.summary: Francois Chollet articulates a conceptual framework that intelligent systems have exactly two adaptation timescales: fast on-the-fly situation modeling (fluid intelligence, realized in modern AI via reasoning/program generation) and slow offline extraction of reusable abstractions from experience buffers (long-term plasticity, realized via pre-training and post-training). He argues that until late 2024, AI lacked the first timescale entirely, relying only on storage and retrieval of training-time patterns. The post references a slide from a recent Berkeley talk.

He frames enterprise AI agents as the new digital front door and notes Sierra now works with nearly 50% of the Fortune 50.

entry.title: Social Summary: November 23, 2026
entry.summary:
Governance dominated the day's discourse. Sam Altman unveiled OpenAI's transparency post proposing industry-wide shared development limits based on perplexity, with Greg Brockman endorsing it and framing around existing White House Accords commitments.

  • Yann LeCun went viral mocking superintelligence hype via the Level-5 driving gap, and separately downplayed AI bio-risk as overestimated
  • The claimed AI-assisted Riemann Hypothesis solution split opinion: Ethan Mollick showed top forecasters badly missed it, while Gary Marcus and LeCun credit the human mathematician over the model
  • François Chollet offered a contrarian economic take: deployment friction may actually benefit AI infrastructure by stretching the datacenter buildout
  • Tunguz ignited a heated legality debate, arguing distillation isn't illegal even on improperly obtained training data
  • Mollick also warned society may retreat from augmentation, and LeCun shared insider history on open-sourcing Llama-2
  • Jeremy Howard celebrated llms.txt adoption in Google Antigravity while critiquing Gemini-4-Neon coding agents for over-engineering

entry.summary: Greg Brockman endorses OpenAI's new transparency post, highlighting its proposal for industry-wide shared safety bars: common limits on pretraining progress measured by perplexity, with concrete exit criteria such as development of a successor to CoT monitors before limits are lifted.

entry.summary: François Chollet argues to Musk and Tan that deployment friction in AI infrastructure may be beneficial: stretching the datacenter buildout over a longer timeline preserves pricing power and gives AI applications time to prove commercial viability, avoiding a capacity spike followed by a glut.

entry.title: "I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to e...

entry.title: Predictions made last MONTH (post Navier-Stokes) about when the Riemann Hypotheses would be solved: ...
entry.summary: Expanding on yesterday's Reddit discussion, Mollick compiles predictions made just a month earlier about when the Riemann Hypothesis would be solved, contrasting Metaculus (May 2035), LEAP superforecasters (10% chance of another Millennium problem solved in 2026), and Terence Tao (humans plus AIs around 2050), implying recent events have outpaced them all.

entry.title: No distillation is illegal on stolen data.
entry.summary: Tunguz posts a pointed aphorism arguing that distillation itself is not illegal even when the underlying training data was obtained without authorization — a provocation in the debate over model distillation and data provenance.

entry.content:
AI-assisted mathematics was the day's dominant story: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed a Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, while Artificial Analysis framed the Millennium Prize Problems as a human-vs-AI scoreboard. Timnit Gebru drew strong engagement criticizing the rushed release over careful 900-page vetting, sustaining healthy skepticism about verification.

  • Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini dominated open-source discussion: Clement Delangue announced the Apache 2.0 release, Artificial Analysis benchmarked the 26B looped MoE, and Soumith Chintala confirmed it runs on 32GB machines
  • OpenAI published original research on combating distillation; Ethan Mollick hypothesized that restricted distillation explains the open-weights slowdown
  • AI-for-science momentum: Demis Hassabis announced an Isomorphic Labs–Merck cancer drug collaboration, and OpenAI shipped MedChemBench plus neurodegenerative disease work
  • Hugging Face's Thom Wolf revealed a proprietary CDN handling exabyte-scale model downloads
  • Google recapped Gemini 4 Neon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen; Greg Brockman showcased GPT-6.2 Astra robotics capability

Overall sentiment blended excitement over AI-for-science breakthroughs and open-source releases with caution about unverified math claims and tightening model security.

A retrospective on the paradigm shift to test-time reasoning.

entry.summary: Demis Hassabis announces a collaboration with Merck on designing a new cancer drug, framing it as a proof point of rapid progress at Iso (Isomorphic Labs) in reimagining drug discovery.

entry.title:
Distillation can reproduce powerful AI capabilities without the safeguards built around them.
We’re...
entry.summary: OpenAI announces new research on combating distillation of its models, examining how capabilities transfer through distillation and how the company detects and disrupts coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities while bypassing built-in safeguards. The findings are intended to strengthen OpenAI's own defenses and support safeguard efforts across the industry.

entry.title:
Millennium Prize Problems: humans and two labs tied with a score of one
➤ Human: Grigori Perelman p...
entry.summary: Artificial Analysis frames the Millennium Prize Problems as a scoreboard: Perelman's recognized Poincaré proof for humanity, OpenAI's claimed September solution to Navier-Stokes using an unreleased internal model, and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge posting a claimed Riemann Hypothesis proof developed with Claude. Notes that P vs NP and several other problems remain open and both AI claims await independent verification.

entry.title:
AI downloads broke the usual CDN model
Since this summer, we're running our own CDN at Hugging Face...
entry.summary: Hugging Face CTO/CO-founder Thom Wolf explains why AI downloads broke traditional CDN design: Hugging Face now runs its own CDN shipping nearly 1 exabyte per month (~420 GB/s across 80,000 req/s), serving few enormous files to machines (GPU clusters) rather than many small files to humans. He details how caching assumptions change for massive objects and release-day traffic floods.

entry.summary: Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue announces that Thinking Machines is releasing Inkling 2 Mini under an Apache 2.0 license, claiming it reaches the Pareto frontier for open agent models, framing it as evidence that American open-source AI remains vibrant.

entry.title: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a...
entry.summary: Artificial Analysis announces Thinking Machines' release of Inkling 2 Mini, a 26B-total/5.4B-active parameter open-weights looped mixture-of-experts transformer scoring 20 on the Intelligence Index, running on a MacBook or DGX Spark, under Apache 2.0 with 1M token context and text/image input.

entry.title: mini model is out. 27B looping MoE, 3B active. fits on a 32GB memory machine. Been running this on m...
entry.summary: Soumith Chintala announces a new small model: a 27B looping MoE with 3B active parameters that fits on a 32GB machine. He reports benchmarking it on DGX Spark and Mac Mini at roughly 75 tok/s decode, notes evals are roughly on par with Qwen 3.8 27B (an existing model released in August), and suggests the local-llama community will be pleased.

entry.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Claude may have just solved the Riemann hypothesis, math's most famous unsolved...
entry.summary: MTS Live reports that Anthropic mathematician Alpoge posted a 4-page note claiming a proof of the Riemann hypothesis working with Claude, formalized as ~250,000 pages of Lean code across 14 machine-checkable files, independently checked by MIT's Andrew Sutherland; a separate 940-page human-only GRH draft by Alessandro Masullo surfaced the same day.
